title: What Made The First Cities Possible
text:
There is a tidy story about the first cities that I want to complicate. In it, agriculture produces a surplus, the surplus frees some people from growing food, and those people become priests, potters and officials, so the city follows automatically from the farm. The sequence sounds logical, but the evidence resists it. Thousands of years separate the earliest farming from the earliest cities, and many farming societies produced surpluses for a very long time without building anything we would call urban.

So what else was required? Several conditions appear together in the river valleys where cities first emerged. Irrigated land could feed dense populations from a small area. Rivers let heavy goods move cheaply, so a settlement could draw on a hinterland far beyond walking distance. Institutions developed that could store grain, settle disputes and compel labour, and those institutions left us temples, granaries and administrative archives. Religion mattered too: many early cities grew up around a shrine that already drew people together for festivals. The lesson is that surplus is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Cities were an achievement of organisation, not an automatic consequence of full granaries.
points: The common story says surplus food frees specialists and a city follows automatically.
That story fails because thousands of years separate early farming from the first cities.
Irrigation allowed dense populations to be fed from a small area of land.
Rivers made it cheap to move heavy goods, extending a settlement's hinterland.
Institutions that stored grain, settled disputes and compelled labour were needed, and religious centres drew people in.
The conclusion is that surplus is necessary but not sufficient; cities were an achievement of organisation.
